title: Tapeworm Infections
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Tapeworms are flatworms that live in the small intestine, causing symptoms from mild abdominal discomfort to severe anemia and neurological deficits. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy and serology, while treatment is anthelmintic therapy with careful monitoring for complications.
aka: Taenia spp., Diphyllobothrium latum, Dipylidium caninum

sections.p: Tapeworms are long, ribbon‑shaped cestodes that attach to the intestinal mucosa. In East Africa, the most common species are Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) and Taenia solium (pork tapeworm).
b: Adult worms live in the small intestine
They can reach several metres in length
They release proglottids that contain eggs

sections.p: Taenia spp. have a scolex with hooks and a rostellum, a broad neck, and a strobila of proglottids. Diphyllobothrium latum is longer, with a smooth scolex and no hooks.
Human ingestion of undercooked beef or pork containing cysticerci leads to adult tapeworms. In T. solium, humans are both definitive and intermediate hosts; pigs are the usual intermediate host.
b: Cysticerci in meat → adult worm in intestine
Eggs passed in stool → contaminate food/water
Intermediate hosts: pigs (T. saginata), cattle (T. saginata), dogs (Dipylidium)

t.b: Detects proglottids or eggs; positive confirms infection
Useful when stool is negative but clinical suspicion high; indicates exposure to antigens
Highly sensitive for species identification when available

sections.p: Most infections are asymptomatic, but complications include abdominal pain, malabsorption, anemia, and in T. solium, neurocysticercosis.
b: Malabsorption of fat and fat‑soluble vitamins

t.b: May show macrocytic anemia if D. latum; eosinophilia in some cases
Low in D. latum infection due to impaired absorption

sections.p: Diagnosis is primarily stool microscopy; repeat samples increase yield. Serology and PCR are adjuncts when microscopy is negative.
b: Three stool samples on consecutive days improve sensitivity

t.b: Detects proglottids or eggs; positive confirms infection
Useful when stool is negative but clinical suspicion high; indicates exposure to antigens
Highly sensitive for species identification when available

sections.p: Praziquantel is first‑line for all tapeworms; albendazole is an alternative. Control focuses on meat inspection, proper cooking, and hygiene.

t.b: Killing adult worms; avoid in pregnancy if possible
Alternative when praziquantel unavailable; avoid in pregnancy

sections.p: Remember that D. latum causes B12 deficiency; T. solium can cause neurocysticercosis. In low‑resource settings, repeat stool exams are essential.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with signs of intestinal obstruction

faq.a: Yes, especially Diphyllobothrium latum can impair vitamin B12 absorption leading to macrocytic anemia.

faq.q: What is the best test if stool microscopy is negative but suspicion remains high?
faq.a: Serology (ELISA) for tapeworm antigens or PCR of stool if available.
It is generally avoided in the first trimester; albendazole is preferred if treatment is necessary.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with chronic abdominal discomfort and weight loss. Stool microscopy is negative. What next? — Repeat stool microscopy on three consecutive days; consider serology if still negative.
A child in a rural village has seizures and a history of eating pork. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Neurocysticercosis due to Taenia solium; confirm with neuroimaging and serology.
A patient with macrocytic anemia is found to have low vitamin B12. Which tapeworm is most likely responsible? — Diphyllobothrium latum; explain the mechanism of B12 malabsorption.

You are treating a patient with a confirmed tapeworm infection in a setting without access to praziquantel. Which drug can you use and why? — Albendazole; it is effective against most tapeworms and safer in pregnancy.
A patient with a tapeworm infection develops severe abdominal pain and vomiting. What emergency condition must you rule out? — Intestinal obstruction or volvulus; urgent imaging and surgical consult.
A patient presents with eosinophilia and a history of swimming in a lake. Which tapeworm is most likely? — Dipylidium caninum; explain the life cycle involving dogs.

You are asked to counsel a community on preventing tapeworm infection. What key points should you emphasize? — Proper cooking of pork and beef, hand hygiene, meat inspection, and avoiding raw fish for D. latum.
